newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - Bulgarian communists promise bright future again.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bulgarian communists promise bright future again.

text.p: Bulgaria's tiny communist party is dusting off its promises of a bright future for the handful of people nostalgic enough to vote for it in Sunday's presidential election.
The communists, whose candidate Vera Ilieva runs a private clinic offering breast and penis enlargements, were ousted in Bulgaria as elsewhere in eastern Europe in 1989.
But after seven years out of power they say they are ready to strike back against "cruel capitalism" and start building the country's communist future again.

"The national currency will be stronger then the dollar, education and health care will be free, the population will grow, the economy will prosper and the country will flourish as it did before the capitalist invasion," party chairman Vladimir Spasov told Reuters after a news conference attended by three journalists and a handful of elderly supporters.

The Bulgarian Communist Party traces its roots back to 1891 and retains its allegiance to communist hero Georgi Dimitrov, one of the leaders of the anti-fascist resistance when Bulgaria was allied to the Axis powers during World War Two.
After 1989, most of Bulgaria's former communists resurfaced in the Bulgarian Socialist Party, which won a majority in parliamentary elections in 1994.

A former anti-fascist guerrilla, Spasov said his party was a "truly Marxist party of a Bolshevik type" and attacked the Socialists as "renegades and traitors" who had abandoned the fight against capitalism to become its main vehicle in Bulgaria.
"Only the Communist Party is able to save the country from economic collapse and lead it to prosperity again, as it was in the communist era," he said.
The communists' promises contrast more than ever with the everyday life of Bulgarians struggling with soaring prices and the collapse of the national currency.

The party even has a plan for nationalising Bulgaria's mafia. Known as "wrestlers", many former sportsmen now use their brawn in crime, working under the cover of some of the hundreds of private security firms.
Spasov said the communists would give them state jobs or pension them off, though he gave no details of how they would be persuaded to comply.

Vice-presidential candidate Iskra Yaneva, a surgeon at the Military Medical Academy, said Ilieva's clinic, far from pandering to the vanity of rich Bulgarians, provided treatments which could help reverse the decline in population.
The National Statistical Institute says emigration and a low birth rate mean Bulgaria's population is expected to fall to 7.1 million in the year 2020 from its present 8.4 million.
"The clinic for plastic surgery owned by our candidate is a humanitarian gesture as it helps sexually impotent Bulgarians to make babies, thereby raising the birth rate," Yaneva said.
Spasov said the clinic would be nationalised under communist rule and all services would be free.

Bulgaria has two million pensioners, many of them nostalgic for the greater security offered by one party rule under former communist leader Todor Zhivkov, when the state ensured cheap bread although blocking freedom of speech and movement.

Newspaper photographs of the 85-year-old ex-dictator always show him smiling and one headline after a recent public appearance suggested he should run for president, though he has said he is too old for a new political career.
Zhivkov was convicted in 1992 of embezzling 21.5 million levs (then about $24 million) of public funds, spent on luxury apartments and Western cars for his family and favoured aides.

He was allowed to serve his seven-year jail sentence at his granddaughter's villa because of his advanced age but he always insisted he was innocent of the charges. In February this year the Supreme Court overturned the sentence.
Thirteen pairs of candidates are contesting Sunday's election and the communists, whose motto remains "Workers of the world unite", are not expected to win more than a handful of votes.
